1) we propose a new parallel algorithm for training ConvNets that can attain linear speedup on multi-core CPUs, 2) we show that our algorithm can attain 90× speed-up on the Xeon Phi™ Knights Core, 3) we show that ZN can be either faster than or slower than certain implementations of ConvNet training on the GPU.
ZNN can (1) attain linear speedup with respect to the number of processors for wide ConvNets, and (2) be either faster or less costly to develop than GPU implementations.

In summary, our research is concerned with
the design and implementation of a parallel algorithm for ConvNet training, and its evaluation on a variety of CPUs.
the development and implementation of a novel algorithm and software package for training 3D ConvNets on shared-memory multi-core and many-core CPUs.
the development of fast and scalable parallel algorithms for training 3D ConvNets.

ZNN can accelerate ConvNet training on CPUs and can attain speedups that are competitive with GPU implementations, and that the ZNN algorithm can be implemented in a straightforward way that is compatible with existing ConvNet software packages.
ZNN is a fast and scalable algorithm for training 3D ConvNets on multi-core and many-core shared memory machines.
ZNN is the fastest algorithm for training ConvNets on CPUs, and that it can also compete with GPU implementations for some network architectures.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
ZNN is a fast and scalable algorithm for training 3D convolutional networks, with performance comparable to or faster than GPUs.
ZNN is an efficient algorithm that can be used to train 3D ConvNets on shared-memory multi- and many-core CPUs, and is a viable alternative to GPU training.
ZNN can train 3D ConvNets on CPUs faster than previous algorithms and is a promising alternative to GPU implementations.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the PRAM speedup is not only a theoretical upper bound, but also can be attained in practice with a simple algorithm.
the ZNN algorithm and implementation can attain good performance on both multi-core CPUs and many-core CPUs, and that it may be a viable alternative for training ConvNets.
the task parallelism of ZNN can be more effective than the SIMD parallelism for CPUs, for the network architectures and convolutional kernels in common use.
